title: Repeated experiences: essential for learning but not always good
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton argues that repeated experiences are what make anything stick in the brain, but that stickiness is indifferent to whether the thing learned is good. Using Wimbledon tennis practice as the positive case, he shows that real repetition means many, many iterations rather than a few. He then offers two cautionary examples: a UK dance television show where harsh coaching taught contestants to feel worthless alongside the steps, and the defeated Conservative government, whose repeated conduct taught voters it was unfit to govern. From these he draws three things that become sticky in any classroom or organisation, namely competence, interest and whether the teacher or manager is on your side. He closes with four questions that providers of repeated experiences should ask themselves.
points: Repetition must be extensive to work, so schools have to find enough time for a lot of repetitions rather than a few token ones.
The brain makes sticky whatever it repeatedly experiences, so bad repeated experiences produce bad learning as reliably as good ones.
Learners are always absorbing three things: whether they are getting better, whether the subject is interesting, and whether their teacher is on their side.
Four self-check questions about quantity, age-appropriateness, shared joy and being on the learner's side give leaders and coaches a practical test.
quotes: Repeated experiences are at the heart of learning. They give the clue to our brains that something has worth. They cause the brain to make those experiences sticky and automatic, saving energy for the future.

In schools and other organisations, time is at a premium. One of the things we have to do is to work out how to provide enough repetitions to help something become sticky, rather than providing a few repetitions that aren’t really worth while.

We talked in some of the earlier posts how the brain is always learning, always making sticky what it repeatedly experiences, for both good and bad. This means that if the repeated experiences are not good, our brains have a very good chance of learning things that are not good.
As a result, some of these celebs have learned dance steps and routines they never knew about before. Unfortunately, they have also learned to feel worthless, unliked, and bullied.
All of these repeated experiences built over time. They helped the electorate to make sticky that the Conservative Party was no longer fit to govern.

Focusing on repeated experiences is exactly what we need to do to enable learning to happen. But that isn’t enough. We have to make sure that the repeated experiences we are creating are producing learning that we want to happen and that is worthwhile and beneficial to our children and students.
